MR. HOWARD    ALLEGED INCOMPLETENESS OF RETURN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege relating to an order of the house passed on May 18, and I read from page 447 of Votes and Proceedings for that day:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General, praying that he will cause to be laid before this house a copy of all correspondence, telegrams and other documents exchanged between the federal government and any person, organization or government, since January 1, 1958, relative to the purchase of land or any other matter relating to the proposed Royal Canadian Mounted Police detachment at Queen Charlotte city.
Sessional paper No. 70-CE contains the correspondence, documents and other material as set out in that particular motion. However, I have reason to believe, sir, there is a letter or document that was sent by the Minister of Justice which is not contained within the file of correspondence made available pursuant to this order of the house.
In this regard I would refer to the Prince Rupert Daily News of Thursday, April 23, 1959, which was within the period covered by the order of the house. In an article on the front page there is an announcement by Mr. A. D. Vance, who is a building supply firm operator and also was Conservative candidate during the last election in the constituency of Skeena, indicating that he had received a communication from the Minister of Justice to the effect that this particular land had been purchased, the price of the land, when construction would begin and so on.
My question of privilege, sir, is that either the Minister of Justice has not put this particular letter or piece of correspondence in the sessional paper or Mr. Vance, who made the announcement in Prince Rupert, is giving to the Minister of Justice some credit which is not due him, that is for writing a particular letter relating to this Royal Canadian Mounted Police detachment at Queen Charlotte city.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a



definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the charge that clandestine political influence has been brought to bear on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation management resulting in the resignation of 12 employees of the corporation, including the supervisor of talks and public affairs, the assistant supervisor of talks and public affairs, C.B.C. radio, and the supervising producer of public affairs, C.B.C. television.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I submit it is clear that this motion is out of order-

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the point of order may I say this. You have not yet put the motion, and perhaps you would follow the normal course of giving the person who moves it a chance to explain it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I have scarcely had time to read the motion which the Leader of the Opposition asks leave to move, but from what he said about it I wonder whether the matter is one which is under the administrative responsibility of the government. I would like to have the Leader of the Opposition address himself to that point. I shall certainly hear the Minister of Justice also. The reason I say that is this. I take it that the motion relates to employees of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is a corporation established by parliament. But as I have heard its relations to the government explained in the house, its responsibility may be directly to parliament. That is the point that strikes me immediately, and on which 1 should be glad to hear the Leader of the Opposition.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are quite right, of course. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a public corporation, but it is responsible to parliament and it reports to parliament through a minister of the crown. In that respect, Mr. Speaker, surely this house is permitted to inquire into matters concerning this corporation, particularly if they affect members of parliament or members of the government. The important part of this motion, it seems to me, is that a charge has been made by those senior officials of the C.B.C. to the effect that, as the motion reads, "clandestine political influence has been brought to bear on the corporation management". It is as a result of that influence, in the view of these officials, that they have been unable to carry on their duties in the way in which they would wish to carry them on. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, surely the fact of resignations of this kind alleged to be brought about by clandestine political influence, will have an unfortunate effect on the integrity and the independence of the C.B.C.

Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I may be permitted to read the statement issued-because it has a bearing on the importance and the urgency of this matter-by the supervisor of talks and public affairs, the assistant supervisor of talks and public affairs and the supervising producer of public affairs, which explains why they felt it necessary to resign, which resignations have been followed by those of other senior officials and I understand the number is increasing. This statement which explains why this course had to be taken is as follows. It was issued, I think, on June 23 and it is signed by the supervisor of talks and public affairs, the assistant supervisor of talks and public affairs and the supervising producer of public affairs, Mr. F. W. Peers, Mr. D. H. Gillis, and Mr. B. Trotter, and reads as follows:
On June 15 C.B.C. management took a decision to cancel the series "Preview Commentary" effective today, June 23. The supervisor of talks and public affairs, Frank Peers, was given no valid reason for this action. The controller of broadcasting, Charles Jennings, handed him a written explanation that the press gallery correspondents who contributed to "Preview Commentary" did not have time to put things in perspective in commenting on the events of the previous day.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, presumably they have time to comment on these things before they send them to their newspapers. The statement goes on:
Since this reason was manifestly absurd applying to professional journalists covering the national capital, Mr. Peers started a series of inquiries which led only to the conclusion that clandestine political influence had been brought to bear on C.B.C. management.
Mr. Speaker, that is not the whole statement but that is the part which I think is relevant to this particular motion. Surely this is a charge which has a bearing on the independence and integrity of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That is something which must be very much in all our minds these days, and it is something which we have a duty in this house to protect. If, Mr. Speaker, this publicly owned and operated corporation is to be subjected to this kind of influence as charged, then not only will it prejudice its existence but it will at the very least put it in an unfavourable position with regard to private broadcasting. The importance of this matter and its seriousness should certainly be apparent to the members of the government, because they took such a strong stand when they were in opposition on the independence and integrity of this corporation and its immunity from any form of influence on the part of the government.
I would now like to quote the words of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) as reported on page 2827 of Hansard

for March 29, 1957, and these will be my final words, Mr. Speaker, to justify not only the importance of this matter but the urgency of discussing it at this time to remove these impressions. The Minister of Finance said:
If the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is to function in a manner free of government interference, then there must not be attempts on the part of the Prime Minister or other members of the government to influence the programming activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and above all opinion broadcasts on public issues.
This resignation statement, Mr. Speaker, alleges that there has been that kind of clandestine political influence, and I suggest it is a matter of importance and urgency and should be discussed immediately.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Before the Leader of the Opposition takes his seat, if debate were permitted on the motion would it directly call into account the administration of the government, or is it a matter for parliament as a whole?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It will call into question the relationship of members of parliament, and particularly members of the government, to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation because of this allegation. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that only by an immediate and reassuring statement from the government in such a discussion as this can the deterioration in the morale of the C.B.C. as a result of resignations of this kind be halted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Perhaps the Minister of
Justice (Mr. Fulton) would prefer to leave his remarks until I have heard the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). He has the floor if he wishes to speak now.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is because I think it is so easily demonstrated that this motion does not comply with the rules that I would appreciate the opportunity to be heard now. There are a number of grounds upon which this motion fails, and I would like to deal with them one by one on the basis of the facts.
First of all I would like to refer to May's fifteenth edition, page 352, which says that the matter raised by the motion must be definite. Your Honour will find that there is a citation there, citation (c), which says that in particular such a motion must not be offered when the facts are in dispute or before they are available. I refer here particularly to the facts being in dispute. My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition has in the wording of this motion itself made it clear that this is a matter of opinion-opinion, I might say, held only by members of the opposition. He

says it is a matter of urgent public importance, namely a charge that clandestine political influence has been brought to bear on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
That is not a fact, Mr. Speaker; this is a matter which is, as I say, based on a charge. The facts in the matter are not established, and therefore the motion does not deal with a definite matter. And to illustrate my point that this is a matter of opinion and dispute only, and indeed to show how unfounded is the charge and how inappropriate would be a discussion of this kind, I should like to refer to a statement dealing with this matter which was made by Mr. Bushnell, general manager and acting president of the C.B.C., which refutes completely the statements the Leader of the Opposition has read into the record. Mr. Bushnell gave the following statement to the press today.
Some two weeks ago the corporation decided to replace the "Preview Commentary" from Ottawa, which followed the eight o'clock C.B.C. news, with a "Special Parliamentary Report" prepared by the C.B.C. news service. It was felt that this would improve the corporation's service of reporting the proceedings of the previous day in parliament.
This has been followed by resignations of several members of the corporation's "Talks and Public Affairs" national office in Toronto, on the grounds that the substitution of the opinion broadcast "Preview Commentary" by the factual C.B.C. news report implied political interference with the C.B.C.'s broadcasting of controversial affairs. The corporation does not accept this implication.
The C.B.C. has the fullest confidence in its talks and public affairs department which over the years has contributed some of the C.B.C.'s most distinguished and responsible broadcasting.
Thus, in so far as the facts are ascertainable, the statement by the responsible manager and acting president completely refutes the charge which has been so baselessly brought in this house by the Leader of the Opposition.
Another ground is that the matter raised in the motion must be urgent, and in this connection there are citations both in Beau-chesne and May, but May deals with this situation very succinctly. I would refer Your Honour to the fifteenth edition at page 352, where it is stated that the motion has been refused where the matter could be raised on the estimates, that is, when an ordinary parliamentary opportunity will occur shortly or in a reasonable time.
I should point out that the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue, who is the minister who answers for the C.B.C., have not yet, I am informed, come before the committee of supply, so there will be ample opportunity to raise this matter and to raise it in the fullest and most satisfactory form in committee of supply when all members may take part in the discussion. On that ground



I think it is obvious, in accord with previous rulings, that the motion fails because the question of urgency of debate does not arise.
Another reason why I submit the motion must fail is one to which you yourself referred, Your Honour, namely that this does not involve the administrative responsibility of the government. May I point out that May, in his fifteenth edition at page 355, gives an example of a somewhat similar motion in the United Kingdom having been ruled out of order on the ground that it related to the conduct of the affairs of a statutory authority. The C.B.C. is set up as a statutory authority. It is a corporation created by parliament. The act which governs it has been carefully drawn to make it clear that the C.B.C. operates as an independent corporation. It does not operate under the direction of the government. It reports to parliament, and is responsible to parliament directly only with respect to its financial requirements. As a statutory authority carefully set apart from the possibility of direct interference by the government, it cannot be said to be under the administrative authority of the government and subject to discussion in these circumstances, under this rule.
May I refer Your Honour to sections 22, 26 and 27 of the Broadcasting Act enacted in 1958. Section 22(1) reads:
There shall be a corporation to be known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Could the minister say what he is reading from?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Yes; the statutes of 1958, the Broadcasting Act.
22. (1) There shall be a corporation to be known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation consisting of a president, a vice-president and nine other directors to be appointed by the governor in council.
Then the other subsections of this section outline the organization of the corporation. Then section 26 (1) provides:
The corporation may on its own behalf employ such officers and employees as it considers necessary for the conduct of its business, at such remuneration and upon such other terms and conditions as it deems fit, but the officers and employees so employed are not officers or servants of Her Majesty.
Then in section 27 it is made clear that the corporation itself is an agent of Her Majesty with all the powers, rights and liabilities usually attached to such crown agencies.
The whole tenor of the statute, and particularly these sections, Mr. Speaker, make it abundantly clear that the corporation is not under the day to day administration of the government. May I in this connection refer Your Honour to a case in the United Kingdom House of Commons, reported in the British Hansard for 1912, volume 41, column 816. This

was a case in which a member moved, or sought leave to move, the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the failure of the board of trade through its representatives to bring pressure to bear on the port authority to carry out its obligations under the port of London act.
In this case the member was seeking to move the adjournment with respect to a matter arising in connection with the port of London authority. The port of London authority was the authority which administered the port of London, and it was a statutory authority in exactly the same way as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is, set up independently of the government although it had to report through the board of trade which, as hon. members know, is the equivalent of the Department of Trade and Commerce in this country. Mr. Speaker immediately ruled as follows:
I regret that 1 am not able to accept the motion of the hon. member. The port of London is an authority set up by parliament and quite independent of the board of trade. I have looked through the act which set up the authority, and I can only find some three sections which introduce the board of trade at all as a controlling authority.
I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that as I recall the Broadcasting Act there is no place at which the Minister of National Revenue or any other minister is introduced as a controlling authority. The Speaker of the British house continued:
Those sections deal with audits if required, with the question of increases of duties, and with complaints about warehousing. As far as I can ascertain, those are the only sections in the bill which give the board of trade any power whatever, or any control over the port authority. That being so, it is clear that the board of trade have no such control as the hon. gentleman would wish to imply in his motion.
From the terms of the Broadcasting Act in Canada, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that neither the Minister of National Revenue nor any other minister of the government had any such control as the Leader of the Opposition seeks to imply in his motion, control over the C.B.C., in a way which would bring it within the rules of parliament as to the content of such motions to adjourn the house.
On these grounds, Mr. Speaker-and there are a number of others which I know will occur to Your Honour, which I therefore think I need not mention today, but particularly on the ground that this is not a definite matter but a matter of opinion, this motion is not in order. The opinion of the Leader of the Opposition is one, I submit, which can clearly be proven to be groundless, but that is a matter, of course, of debate-on these grounds, it is not in order to introduce charges,

to raise matters of this kind which really involve charges against the government based on opinion, on a motion seeking to debate a definite matter of urgent public importance.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have often heard the Minister of Justice in the past when he appeared to be on much stronger ground than he is this afternoon. As a matter of fact I think his argument is particularly weak. He says this is not a definite matter. I do not know whether you have to have some physical object which can be weighed before you have a definite matter. This is a definite charge that has been made in writing by no less a person than the leader of the official opposition in this house, and I think it is very much a definite matter, since it charges that clandestine political influence has been brought to bear on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
To make it something that is most definite one need only to keep in mind the continuing reports of further resignations from the C.B.C. I understand that now there have been in excess of 20 resignations. When people are resigning in very large numbers apparently in protest of the definite matter that has been set forth in this motion, is this not a definite matter? In my submission, Mr. Speaker, this is something that is a very definite matter, which has been well set out in the motion.
It has been said by the Minister of Justice that this is not urgent; that it can be debated when the estimates of the department are before the house. That, of course, is true, but there is no assurance as to how soon those estimates will be before the house for debate. They may be the last estimates in the dying days of the session. In the meantime, how many more resignations may there be from the C.B.C.? I think it is urgent that this be discussed so the matter may be aired fully and so that a further deterioration of the C.B.C. itself may not take place, if such an assurance is in fact given.
I think the whole question of interference by the government in the administration of the C.B.C. is not only a definite and urgent matter but it is something of very great concern to the people of this country, in that it suggests that there has been political interference with freedom of discussion through the C.B.C. I suggest that it is such an important and far-reaching matter that it deserves immediate debate.
The Minister of Justice brought forward many citations to endeavour to prove that the C.B.C. is beyond the administrative jurisdiction of the government. The point of this motion, I suggest, is that, while everyone agrees that this is what the law says, nevertheless even with that situation as it is set

forth there is the charge of political interference. It is a very grave and a very serious charge that has been presented, namely that in spite of the safeguards in the laws of this country there has been political interference. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in this whole question is the matter of freedom of discussion, freedom of the C.B.C., apart from government and cabinet interference. For all these reasons urgency of debate is essential.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I
should say a word or two, not that it is necessary-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Before the minister begins, since he is the responsible minister, I take it that he is addressing himself to the question of standing order 26, and whether a debate should be allowed on the issue?

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
It is not necessary to supplement the argument which was advanced by the Minister of Justice, which I am sure is sound and valid and which I should hope would commend itself to your judgment when you make your ruling, Your Honour.
The Minister of Justice referred to the fact that the estimates of the corporation have not yet been before the committee. That is true. There may be some merit in the suggestion that those estimates could possibly be deferred for some little while, but I would point out that the committee on broadcasting, which is charged particularly with the investigation of this corporation, is meeting today in Toronto, where the directors of the corporation are meeting, and will resume sittings here on either Monday or Tuesday of next week. I would also point out that one of the responsibilities of that committee, of course, is to investigate fully all affairs of the C.B.C. I think that is one answer to the question of urgency of debate, and supplements the information with respect to estimates.
I certainly appreciate the information I have received this afternoon. It has been said by one member that there have been 12 resignations and by another that there have been 15, and if two or three more members get up we may have 30 or 40. As far as the management is concerned, and I am speaking now of the manager with whom I talked just before coming into the house, the figures on resignations are in no way similar to those which have been detailed to the house.
I want to point out that this charge is based on what the Leader of the Opposition says is a statement from the corporation. I suggest that statements from the corporation



come from the management of the corporation, and a statement by the management of the corporation was read by the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
May I be
allowed to say a word in answer to what the minister has said, particularly having regard to the statement that the estimates might well be discussed in the near future. That is a point that repeatedly comes up when a motion is made to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance. Earlier we were told that the reason a matter was not urgent was that it could be discussed on a supply motion, and this time we are told it is not urgent because the estimates will come up in due course. These, sir, are not the criteria on which the matter should be disposed of, because the rule in Beauchesne makes it quite clear upon what formalities the motion should be based.
My hon. friend also made reference to the committee on broadcasting. We all know that if this matter is to be disposed of by the committee on broadcasting it cannot be done on Monday, for the simple reason that these people would have to receive notice and it would probably be a week before they could come down here, so that again falls to the ground.
But the main point made by the Minister of Justice was that this was not a definite matter. What could be more definite, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia, than the resignation of a number of top officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? On that basis alone, which indicates that there is interference not only there but elsewhere in connection with the corporation, I submit this is a matter which should be debated at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The urgent matter which is proposed is that clandestine political influence has been brought to bear on the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is the charge.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The charge is that that has been done. It has been urged that it is not a definite matter. In my view there are definite facts. There is the fact of resignations and the statement made by those who have resigned, which seems to me to be fairly definite. It is a matter of urgent public importance, of course, because it involves the independence of the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Therefore I am prepared to go that far with the Leader of the Opposition who asks for leave to discuss this matter.
The question of urgency is not, I think, conclusive. There will be an opportunity to

discuss these matters on the estimates, but this matter has arisen suddenly and if it complies with the rule on other grounds I think I would be prepared to accept the request for leave to discuss it as a matter of urgent public importance.
My difficulty lies in the question of whether it really involves the administration of the government. It involves the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Apparently the conduct of the management has been such that certain members have resigned. The charge is that there has been clandestine political interference. I can only go on what is before me, and it is not a charge that the administration has been guilty of clandestine interference with the management. In fact, the management as it has been established under the Broadcasting Act, is an independent management.
I am impressed with the reference the Minister of Justice made to a decision with respect to the port of London authority and I ask the house whether, if this motion is debated, its effect would be that the administration should interfere with the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Otherwise the motion is futile. There is no point in the house debating this as an administrative responsibility unless the purpose is to ask the administration to interfere with the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which, as I understand it, they have at all times resisted doing.
In the absence of a charge that the administration has been interfering with the management, which it seems to me would raise a matter for debate, I cannot accept the application for leave as it stands.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of National Revenue if he has in any manner whatsoever had discussions with or made representations to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation regarding a program entitled "Preview Commentary", and can he tell the house why it has been decided to discontinue this program?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision was one of management. I knew nothing about it until this morning, when I heard on the radio that this decision had been made. That was the first intimation I had of it, and I also heard of the resignations.
As most hon. members know, the directors are meeting in Toronto. That was arranged weeks ago, and the directors have come

from all parts of Canada to inspect the facilities of the C.B.C. and to talk with the senior officers of the corporation in Toronto during the last two days. I immediately tried to get in touch with Mr. Bushnell. I did not reach him until around 11.30 because he was at meetings. He then dictated to me the statement which my colleague the Minister of Justice has put on the record. That is my knowledge of this matter.

May I ask the
minister if he will be good enough to answer my first question. Has the minister in any manner whatsoever had discussions with or made representations to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation regarding the program entitled "Preview Commentary".

I have had discussions from time to time with the manager and Mr. Ouimet before his illness about various C.B.C. programs, as to costs and so on and so forth. I do not remember discussing this particular program. If I did I expressed my appreciation of it, because it is a program for which I have had a very high appreciation. I have made no representations to the C.B.C., directly or indirectly, at any time or at any place, with respect to any program of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, in our further prospecting to secure the facts I wish to ask the Minister of National Revenue another question somewhat related to the one asked by the former minister of national health and welfare, now the farmer expert for Essex East.
In view of reports that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is planning to cancel its morning radio preview commentary; in view of reports that the C.B.C. has been under pressure from Progressive Conservative senators and backbench M.P.'s; and in view of the reported resignation of a number of news commentators, can the minister do anything to enlighten the house as to the drama being played behind the curtain of official silence while the orchestra of public opinion continues to play that old tune, "Tell Me One thing but Tell Me True"?

Whatever merit there may be in the question of the hon. member, we always appreciate the poetic atmosphere and the language in which it is expressed. There has been no drama played behind the scenes of which I have knowledge, and I am sure if there were I would have knowledge of it. There is a reference in the hon. member's question to backbench members, whoever they may be, and some senators. I would
Inquiries of the Ministry appreciate elucidation and the identity of these people, if the hon. member has any information which he can give me.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON METEOR- OLOGICAL SERVICE AND WEATHER FORECASTS FOR FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Gloucester inquired as to what specific meteorological service is provided to warn fishermen of approaching storms, and also asked if warning was given of the sudden storm over the Northumberland strait area last Friday.
I am advised by my officials that marine forecasts giving advice on present weather conditions and forecasts for the next 24 hours are issued three times a day for Canadian coastal waters and most of the larger inland lakes. Whenever observed weather conditions indicate that a special marine weather warning of gales, icing and the like should be issued, such warnings are issued and distributed as soon as possible. These warnings are distributed mainly by radio.
Specific warnings were issued by the Halifax and Gander forecast offices during Friday evening, but the fishing vessels, because of the salmon run, had put out much earlier than usual and the warnings were not issued until 8.45 p.m. at Halifax and

Inquiries of the Ministry 9 p.m. at Gander. This timing was due to difficulties in interpretation of changes in blocked weather systems in northwestern and western Canada, where a change in relatively stationary conditions over previous days was developing, and was also due to scarcity of information as to weather reports from ships in the eastern area.
The storm moved in rapidly from the southeast, and the strength of the winds reported over the maritimes was a great deal higher than any previously observed and reported winds emerging from the gradually changing weather conditions mentioned. The afternoon forecast carried at 5 p.m. did not anticipate the severity of the winds experienced, since local storms resulting from this type of situation can move very suddenly.
A full report is being prepared to cover the weather situation as it was, and a detailed research study is being undertaken so that weather offices will be in a better position to anticipate such unusual and rapid weather developments.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PROVISIONS
speechtext:
This clause might be a little long to explain. In subclause 1 a contributor who, having reached retirement age, ceases to be a member of the forces for any reason other than disability or misconduct is entitled to a benefit. That benefit is determined by the following subparagraphs. I have no quarrel with subparagraph (a). I have no quarrel with subparagraph (b), but I want to read it anyway:
If he has served in the forces for more than three years but less than ten years, he is entitled to
(i)	a return of contributions, or
(ii)	a cash termination allowance, whichever is the greater; and
(c) if he has served in the forces for ten or more years, he is entitled to an annuity.
Subclause 2 deals with a member of the forces who is compulsorily retired because he has become disabled, and the benefits to which he is entitled are the same as in subclause 1. What I have some quarrel with is subclause 3, which reads as follows:
A contributor who, not having reached retirement age, is compulsorily retired from the forces to promote economy or efficiency is entitled to a benefit determined as follows;
(a) if he has served in the forces for three years or less, he is entitled to a return of contributions;
Then (b) deals with service of more than three years but less than ten years, and the benefit is a return of contributions or a cash termination allowance, whichever is the greater. I have some quarrel with subparagraph (c) of subclause 3. This reads as follows:
(c)	if he has served in the forces for ten or more years but less than twenty years, he is entitled-
And subparagraph (i) deals with those members of the forces who served in world war II. Then:
(ii) in the case of any other contributor, to an annuity, reduced, until such time as the contributor reaches sixty-five years of age but not thereafter, as follows:
Then (A) and (B) give the reduction of the benefit.
(d)	if he has served in the forces for 20 or more years, he is entitled to an annuity.
I have read all this to make the following point. If a member of the force is retired because he has reached the retirement age he is entitled to some definite benefit as enumerated in subsection 1. If he retires because he is disabled he is entitled to the same benefit and he has an option-I am speaking now of those members of the forces who have served for less than 10 years or for 10 or more years. Under subsection 3 these members of the forces are put on retirement because the forces do not need them for one reason or another, either because

there is a reduction in the numbers in the force, or to promote efficiency or economy, as is set out in line 5 on page 12.
It seems to me that those members who are retired through no fault of their own are penalized, because they have lost options and lost benefits, compared with those who retire because they are disabled or because they have reached the retirement age. There are other sections later in the act which deal with misconduct, those who are tried by court martial and so on. Would the minister think of this and give us an idea why there is such a difference?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PROVISIONS
speechtext: The reason is that an actuarial balance is required, and in these cases the men have not served their full length of time. They have been retired for various reasons; maybe there is no further employment for them in their particular class of work. There are a variety of reasons, and it is to deal with situations of this kind that these minor modifications to the pension plan are introduced.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PROVISIONS
speechtext: I will take for example the case of a man who has served for 10 or more years. Under subsection 2, subparagraph (b) this man is retired because he is disabled, and he is entitled, I understand, to full annuity which may vary depending on the number of years he has served. I take next a man under subsection 3 who has served for 10 or more years. He retires. I will not say he is thrown out; he retires, say, to promote efficiency and economy, and this man is not entitled to the same benefit, so he is penalized through no fault of his own. He is not disabled, and he has not reached the retirement age, but still he is retired under compulsion and receives less benefit than the other man who has reached the retirement age or is disabled.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PROVISIONS

What kind of work is he going to do in these days of unemployment, or now that he has reached a certain age when employers normally may not want him because he is too old or because he has no experience in trade or business? He is out on the sidewalk. I really
Defence Services Pension Act do think this man is penalized because he is retired from the force through no fault of his own.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PROVISIONS
speechtext:
This was given very careful
consideration. In the Public Service Superannuation Act there is what is called the

deferred annuity; that is, a man who is retired at an earlier age, for some reason or another, does not receive any pension until he reaches the age of 60. As far as the armed forces are concerned, he may get a termination allowance. Now, that is an immediate payment. The reason the armed forces did not wish to adopt the same system as the public service was the feeling that a great many men who have been in the armed forces have lived a life in barracks and have not learned a trade which will enable them to get established immediately on going into civilian life. By getting an immediate payment they are enabled to carry over during the period when they are searching for employment, or it gives them a certain amount of money to establish themselves in some private business. It was for this reason that the armed forces preferred to have this type of immediate payment rather than having a pension deferred until they reached the age of 60.
I think if the hon. member will consider conditions as they exist in the services in peacetime he will agree that this is probably the better system for these men who have to go out and who have not any particular trade or profession in which they may go.

speechtext: In explanation I would point out that the purpose of clause 19 of the bill is to permit a civil servant or a member of the R.C.M.P. who becomes a member of the regular forces, and thus a contributor under the proposed Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, to transfer to this latter act all of his public or R.C.M.P. service and prior military service which he was entitled to count under the Public Service Superannuation Act or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act as applicable. Farm Improvement Loans Act to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Furthermore, I intend to direct certain questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when the house is in committee.
On June 15 last, while the house was considering the resolution to amend the act, we were glad to hear the minister commend that bill.
After explaining why the act had been adopted, the minister quoted figures which fully vindicate the advantages contemplated by that legislation. In fact, as recorded on page 4736 of Hansard, he stated:
Loans under the act during 1958 totalled 70,278 in number, and $90,539,743 in amount borrowed. This represents an increase in lending of approximately $20 million over the amount lent during each of the preceeding three years.
The minister also told the house that the increase was much more substantial for the first three months of 1959, when loans had increased from $10,436,991 to $14,707,086, that is an increase of 40 per cent. He stated further that there was every reason to believe that in 1959 those loans would reach an unprecedented volume.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take too much of the house's time in analysing the report made by the minister and saying all the good I think about the proposed legislation. Besides, it has already been commended by the minister himself when he said, as recorded on page 4736 of Hansard:
The figures give some indication of the credit service which has been rendered to Canadian agriculture through this legislation. The credit has been available and utilized in all provinces.
We, in the province of Quebec, are happy to be able to enjoy the benefits of an act passed in 1934 under a Liberal government, of which the Hon. James Ilsley, then minister of finance, and the Right Hon. Mr. Gardiner, then minister of agriculture, were members.
It is to the latter, especially, that we owe all the agricultural legislation which gave our farmers the prosperity they have known during the post-war years. I am convinced that the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) agrees with me.
If our farmers have increased their loans, can it be due to an improvement in farming conditions? No, Mr. Speaker, because they have run into debt to the tune of $40 million in 1957 and 1958, and of over $14 million in the first three months of 1959.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness), saw fit to announce, on various


occasions, that the increase of agricultural production was 8 per cent higher than the year before. However, he did not say by what amount farmers went into debt during the same period.
Apart from having incurred debts to the amount of $54 million under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, farmers have also increased their liability to the extent of $61 million under the Canadian Farm Loan Act. During the last three years, loans granted by the board were $8.2 million for 195556, $13.2 million in 1956-57, $19.3 million in 1957-58, and $29 million for the year 1958-59.
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in giving those figures was to show the house that the farmers' position is not as rosy as the Ministers of Agriculture and Finance have indicated. Farmers are getting deeper into debt from year to year, so much so that many of them will be bankrupt within the next few years, if their position does not improve.
Mr. Speaker, I realize I am not allowed to dwell on this subject or to discuss the farmer's position. However, I reserve the right to revert to this matter when the proposed amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act come up for debate.
I just wanted to say that we have a long way to go to restore to farmers the confidence they had before the Conservative government took over.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we are supporting this bill. If I had to reproach the Minister of Finance with anything about it, it would be his failure to introduce this legislation sooner, considering that the fiscal year ended on March 31 last. We are now at the end of June, banks have continued making loans and we are asked to pass legislation that expired on March 31 of this year. If it is decided to change that legislation next year, I hope the Minister of Finance will submit amendments early in the session.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howard for the second reading of Bill No. C-16, to amend the Canada Elections Act (absentee voting).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill was considered for the first time at this session, for the first time since the government changed two years ago, I believe, and possibly for the first time in the history of parliament, on March 10 of this year. If I may trespass very briefly on the time of the house, perhaps it would be useful, before getting into general observations on the principle of the bill, to point out exactly what the bill attempts to do.
As the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), the sponsor of the bill, pointed out on March 10, this particular amendment to the Canada Elections Act should not be confused with another amendment standing in his name dealing with advance polls. The absentee voting provided for in this particular measure is not the advance voting provided for in the other measure standing in the hon. member's name. The provisions of this bill would enable one to vote somewhere else on the normal election day. Advance polls, of course, are held before the general election day.
The hon. member had a precedent in proposing this particular measure for our consideration in the practice carried out in two western provinces, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. To a limited extent the right
Canada Elections Act
of absentee voting exists in the province of Ontario but I understand it pertains only to mariners who may be absent from their particular riding on election day. The bill provides two different forms of ballot to take advantage of absentee voting. One is an ordinary ballot for people who may find themselves in the riding on election day but remote from the poll where they would normally be expected to vote. I presume this would apply in the case of very large ridings such as we have in the northern and northwestern part of the country and I can see that it might also be of value in a riding such as I represent which stretches approximately 120 miles along the coast of Nova Scotia and where one might be in Ecum Secum and entitled to vote at Hubbards at the other end. That is one of the ballots proposed in the measure introduced by the hon. member.
The second is a special blank ballot which is for use outside the constituency under the formula set forth in the bill. There may be some confusion with respect to ballot form 36A which is printed as part of the schedule to the bill in that there are two blank spaces on that ballot. As all hon. members know, there are two ridings in Canada which are dual-member constituencies. I have the honour to represent one, the constituency of Halifax, where one is entitled to vote for two members on election day. The other is the riding of Queens in Prince Edward Island.
The blank ballot that is proposed for the absentee voter could of course give rise to problems in single member ridings where, unless there is a great deal of public education on the matter, the absentee voter might think he had hit a bonanza and was entitled to vote for two members instead of one, absence making the heart grow fonder, so to speak, of all politicians. It is not a danger to be fond of all politicians but it is a danger to lose your vote by voting for too many politicians. However, my observation is perhaps of the picayune variety and any danger could be cured when the bill reaches committee by deciding that the ballot should have a single blank space for single member constituencies and a double blank space for double member constituencies.
The formula offered to us by the hon. member for Skeena in presenting the measure is that absentee voting should be confined to those people who are in a province adjacent to the one in which they are resident. This would be of great advantage to the people of the maritimes. Each one of our three provinces is adjacent to the others. Elsewhere in Canada, a person from Ontario would have a chance to vote in Quebec or Manitoba but that is all. A New Brunswick

Canada Elections Act
man who was absent from the province on election day could vote in Quebec, Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia. He would have three chances, as it were, three places where he could vote instead of two. I will say something about the adjacent province formula a little later.
One other proposal made in the bill before us this afternoon is that nomination day take place 28 days in advance of polling day. It is usually 14 days except in certain areas which are most isolated. I must confess that I do not follow the reasoning of the hon. member in making this proposal.
We all grant that the right to vote is one of the most important rights that citizens in a democracy enjoy and at first blush it would seem very important that we do all we can to see that the vote is as heavy as possible. In proposing this measure the hon. member for Skeena will certainly ensure that there will be at least a few thousand votes added in every riding, votes of people who for some reason or another are unable to be at home on election day. I am sure most members would agree that if the case were as simple as that it would be a very good thing for us to have a system of absentee voting in Canada.
Other approaches toward solving the problem of the absentee voter commend themselves. For example, a voter may be away on business and I thought one approach would be to declare election day a holiday, as it is for certain people, or declare it a bank holiday so that the ordinary business of the country would cease and everybody would be free to go to the polls. The danger of that approach is that if you declare a holiday everybody will immediately go forth to their pleasures, and instead of building up the vote you would probably simply build up the necessity for some system of absentee voting.
Another approach, and again this is not the method used by the hon. member, would be to set forth some list of exemptions of those who would be entitled to use the absentee vote. He has done this in a certain respect, in that a person has to show some cause for being unable to be at his poll on election day and therefore asking to use another poll or, if outside the province, a blank ballot.
These are three approaches, and the one he has chosen is to use the adjacent province formula, mixed in with some show of cause as to why the voter is absent from the place he would be normally expected to vote. My problem, Mr. Speaker, is that I could not make up my mind when the measure was debated on March 10 as to what approach I should take to this problem. When I rose to speak at that time the whip of the Liberal

party said I had one minute, so there was not much time to make up my mind. It is a far cry from March 10, but I am still unable to make up my mind whether or not this is really a good measure. The problem I face, Mr. Speaker, is that I am not sure whether or not this is a cheapening of the democratic process.
The right to vote has been a hard fought one; blood has been spilled and heads have been knocked in. People have gone to their graves to ensure that there shall be a democratic process in Canada and in other countries. Now, we are taking this hard fought right to vote, one of our most precious rights, and we are, in effect, debasing it somewhat in making it as available as all the attractive groceries that line the shelves of a supermarket. We are saying to a person that it is possible to feel free to roam at election time because upon showing good cause he will be able to vote. I am sure that the "good cause" would be construed in a generous rather than a narrow sense. I am sure there would be hundreds of people who would take advantage of the opportunity. I feel that this approach to voting does tend to cheapen the value of a particular vote.
However, that is not going to be my main consideration in announcing my decision in due course toward this bill. I should like to hear arguments on the point I have just presented. Perhaps those who follow me in the debate would be good enough to help clear up the doubts that are in my mind about it. There was one point made by one of the previous speakers, and I think the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) raised it by way of a question rather than by any speech of his own. He asked whether there was not a danger that the election results might be rather inconclusive on election night because there would still be these absentee votes to be counted. This happens in any close race now because the armed services' vote is not brought into the final tally until some days or weeks later. I suggest to the hon. member for York-Scar-borough, who raised the question, that it is really answered by comparing the absentee vote to the armed services vote in that respect.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, it is time to make up my mind as to whether or not I am in favour of this measure. I think perhaps I am not, but I would give it support here if I could be convinced that this method of making voting easier is not a means of debasing the sacred right of the ballot. (Translation):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions in the past, though I am not terribly old, I have had to

sacrifice a trip and to postpone important business to wait tor polling time in my constituency, because I made it a point to fulfil what I consider as an important duty for any responsible citizen who has regard for our democratic way of life.
I know that a great many people have been doing the same, and I also know that a great many citizens will not bother to vote if it interferes with some immediate pleasure or task.
We find that, under certain circumstances, candidates are elected by an active minority, while large numbers of voters do not bother to vote. This is, of course, a lack of responsibility on the part of people who feel free to criticize those who take on the task of managing the country's business. Indeed, I understand that in some countries, it has been necessary to make voting compulsory, and to force citizens to meet their obligation.
Mr. Speaker, I know I would be out of order in wandering off too far into the field of compulsory voting, but perhaps you will allow me to point out that it is a shame to see so many people show so little consideration for a right that was gained at the cost of untold sacrifices, and often, indeed, through revolt and bloodshed.
Even in Canada, we had to fight tooth and nail to gain the right to vote and to enjoy responsible government, and I think it is because of the carefree life we are used to, and the freedom we enjoy, that people today hardly bother about casting their vote.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to support Bill C-16, as introduced by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I think if this amendment to the Elections Act were passed, fewer people would find an excuse for failing to vote.
In the last election, for instance, I know of scores of people who apologized in advance for being unable to vote because they were planning a trip. Others, travelling salesmen, were unable to take advantage of advance polls, because the rules governing such polls are so strict that very very few people can qualify. I do not have the figures here, but in a constituency such as my own, where there are over 33,000 people on the voting list, less than 15 per cent were able to use the advance poll.
Mr. Speaker, I am even wondering whether the hon. member has gone far enough in proposing to open up the polls only to people 66968-9-321
Canada Elections Act
travelling in adjacent provinces. Personally,
I think every Canadian citizen should be entitled to vote anywhere in Canada. Indeed I would even suggest that those who travel abroad should have an opportunity to vote by calling at the closest Canadian consular office.
An example of this method has been given by the French republic which, in its last referendum, succeeded in getting its citizens in foreign lands to vote, and indeed in getting the vote from French citizens who have since then become citizens of other countries.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I favour the principle of any measure aimed at promoting the exercise of the right to vote, and the normal functioning of democracy; it gives me pleasure, therefore, to lend my support to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Skeena.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to take part in the debate on Bill C-16.
I fully agree with the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Brassard) in his statement that the right to vote is a privilege and a duty that every citizen should exercise on polling day. However, I feel that it is a privilege that people normally ignore.
In fact, in the recent Ontario elections, only 64 per cent of registered voters cast their vote.
In the last general elections, over 83 per cent of the voters in my constituency cast their votes. I think this is practically a record.
Across the river, in the constituency of Winnipeg South Centre, 80 per cent of the voters cast their votes, while the turnout in Bonavista-Twillingate was only 75 per cent.
In my opinion, this bill is somewhat too complicated. In my view, the right to vote should not be exercised outside the province itself, because so few voters exercise that privilege. In my opinion, it would be quite difficult to conduct an election in that way.
The advance polls now provided are little used. For instance, in St. Boniface, 78 voters out of a total of 35,000, exercised their right to vote on the appointed days. In Winnipeg South Centre, only 66 voters out of 53,443, voted at the advance polls.
Besides, when you study those figures you find that voters at advance polls generally

Canada Elections Act
vote the same way as the majority of voters in the constituency. For instance, in Winnipeg South, where the Conservative majority was considerable, 45 voters favoured the Conservative party, 14 the Liberal party and 7 the C.C.F. party.
Now, in St. Boniface, out of 78 who voted at advance polls, 34 supported the Conservative party, 26 voted C.C.F. and 17 voted Liberal.
I said just now that the procedure proposed in this bill would be too complicated because people are not even interested in voting, even if, in many cases, their polling station is only a few hundred yards away.
To exercise his right of vote, under this bill, the elector will have first to apply for a ballot paper from the returning officer's office of his electoral district. Then, he would have to get a witness to identify him in the poll where he would vote. In addition, he would have to sign an affidavit, and the person who would accompany him would also have to take the oath. I believe that few people would willingly submit to all those requirements.
However, if some easier procedure could be devised, perhaps I might support the bill.
Besides, it would be necessary, under the bill, that the nomination be held 28 days before election day; under the Canada Elections Act as it now stands, the delay is only 14 days. I believe the suggested system would make elections almost impossible.
Then, too, it would be difficult to get the results on the election day and I believe this practice could lead to certain abuses and allow certain people to vote who are not entitled to do so. Even under the system we now have, fraudulent practices often creep in at election time.
Personally, I believe that we should favour the advance polling system within the ridings themselves, for the benefit of travellers who have to be away from their homes on voting day. I believe that in this way we could give practically all the electors the right to vote in their own constituency, provided they have proper identification, even if their name were not on the voters' list. But, I think it would be a little exaggerated to give the right to vote in another province thus allowing a person from Manitoba to vote here in Ottawa, or in Saskatchewan and so on. When electors show that they appreciate the privilege of

voting by turning out in a proportion of 90 per cent, for instance, perhaps we might then endeavour to find a system to facilitate the exercise of the right to vote.
