subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think most hon. members realize full well that we are dealing with a most important subject. I feel that all hon. members have the idea that one thing of which we in Canada can be proud is our electoral system. I believe this idea receives the support of most hon. members.
For my part as a member of this house I know that whether I won or lost an election I have always been extremely happy about the way in which the electoral officers have run affairs in my district. Hence, not unlike most hon. members, anything that we do with regard to electoral laws, I look upon as being an extremely important matter. Consequently the first thing I ask myself in relation to a bill of this nature is this: How practical is it in an administrative sense? Actually I think that is one thing that is basically in the minds of all of us this afternoon: Can a law of this type, if it is passed by this House of Commons, be administered in a practical way?
Frankly, I may say that is the question that I have been asking myself ever since I realized that I would have the opportunity of speaking on this subject. I appreciate the fact that most of the clauses of this bill have received a great deal of study. I congratulate hon. members opposite on the preparation they have put into this bill. From the very nature of the draftsmanship of the bill it is obvious that it has received a great deal of consideration and study. At the same time, even after reading it I again return to the fact that I question the possibility of administering it. I know that we want, in a democracy like Canada, to make it possible for as many people to vote as possible, and I will have something later to say about the remarks, with which I fully agree, made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) about the fact that voting does involve certain sacrifices.
Against that consideration I think we should in this modern day and age of communications realize that by and large it is desirable to have as many people as possible voting. Like most hon. members of this house, Mr. Speaker, I only have my own particular constituency to go by when

discussing a bill of this nature. I know that the population of my own area, Brome-Missisquoi, is a little over 40,000, and there are approximately 22,000 on the electoral list. I have always said to myself that it seems a relatively small number of people on a list considering the total population, in view of the fact that I know full well that the enumerators in my particular area, undoubtedly, like most areas, do a very thorough job. In my area the generation of young people is considerable; in other words, I have an area where families are very large. Even so I suspect that the list of voters could be a little larger under certain conditions. Whether or not certain people decide not to go to the trouble of voting, or even decide not to let their names get onto an electoral list because they are going to travel on election day, is a question I cannot answer. I would like to ask members opposite if they have any statistics for this particular dilemma in which I find myself, because it is a question I cannot decide on.
I know, that in my own area many people phoned our organizers, as they must have phoned the organizers of members opposite, and asked them how they might vote in an advance poll because on election day they would be travelling. Although in the last election many, many provisions were made for voting at advance polls, I personally was surprised-and whether or not it was because the law is basically complicated I do not know-at the number of people who actually availed themselves of the privilege of voting at an advance poll. No doubt a person has to be most sincere in his desire to want to exercise his democratic franchise, and go to the trouble of asking questions and usually travelling a little further than he would normally do, on advance poll day. Many people kept coming up to me before election day and asked these questions, and I still feel that there is no doubt a bill of this nature could, as the hon. member for Halifax said, get more people on the list voting on election day.
I was more than interested in the remarks which he made about the double constituencies in the province of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and I certainly hesitate to feel that a bill of this nature should prejudice the ridings which he mentioned. Undoubtedly no such thing was in the minds of members opposite. I am not suggesting that for a moment, but I would like to reiterate the problem which the hon. member brought up in relation to the double constituencies. I point this out only to make sure that this very knotty problem was in the 66968-9-321J
Canada Elections Act
minds of members opposite when they took the trouble to draft this particular piece of legislation.
In reading over this bill I am sure I have asked myself, generally speaking, some questions that most hon. members have asked themselves. For example, should we make it too easy for a citizen to vote? Should we not, in the truest sense of the word, make some sort of sacrifice on voting day? The thought came to my mind that many people would simply say, "Well, we can take a holiday; we can go and travel in any part of the country and still have our right to vote." Frankly, I do not think this bill intends to permit that sort of thing, and for that reason the legislation which is being contemplated at the present moment should actually consider a means test. In other words, the advance poll rules and regulations should specify those people who are going to be allowed to use the privileges of this type of vote. Thus I think it is very important that this particular legislation which we are considering contemplates the fact that only certain people in certain forms of activity can avail themselves of the particular privileges which are contemplated in this legislation. I think it is most important that this be considered, and once more I reiterate the fact that I do not think this legislation should, or even does, visualize the possibility of Mr. X or Mr. Y going on a long pleasure trip on election day and exercising his vote in that way.
Mr. Speaker, the points which I have brought up do indicate in no small way that there might be, as I said at the opening of my remarks, certain administrative difficulties in administering an act of this sort. As I said, most hon. members are well aware of the efficiency of the marvellous electoral system in this country, and I have the feeling that this is one thing which might certainly have been advanced by the chief electoral officer had it seemed practicable.
The hon. member for Halifax mentioned what he called the general neighbouring province rule in this bill, and I not know whether or not it is a little discriminatory. I do not see why, for instance, we cannot visualize the possibility of a travelling salesman from Nova Scotia finding himself in British Columbia on election day. No doubt if he is really travelling on business as a travelling salesman and just has to be in British Columbia, as a voting resident of the province of Nova Scotia I personally see no reason why he should be excluded from voting under this particular type of legislation. It seems to me that he is one of those cases which this legislation should help, and that is why I ask whether or not the general

Canada Elections Act
neighbouring province rule which was enunciated by members opposite should be considered.
These certainly are considerations which I felt were pertinent and which I felt should be brought up at the present time as we consider most important measures in relation to an electoral system which I for one, in conjunction with our parliamentary system of government, feel is perhaps second to none in the western world.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill that is before us this afternoon attempts to deal with the problem that arises from the increasing mobility of our people in our type of civilization. Many of the occupations and activities of our people take place outside their constituencies and the places in which they reside most of the year. This is an extension of the principle which has been adopted to permit members of the armed forces to vote while they are away from home. It would permit groups such as construction workers and others who cannot get back home in order to vote in their home constituencies; it would benefit those who cannot benefit at present under the advance poll regulations, in that they will not be in their constituency at the time the advance poll is open, to vote on polling day in the location where they may be, although the bill does limit this opportunity to voting in their own provinces or in adjacent provinces; for example, someone living in Ontario could vote if he were in Quebec or Manitoba.
I think this expresses the good intention of making it possible for the maximum number of qualified voters to vote wherever they may be in order to enable them to exercise that franchise which is so important and sacred to them. I think it is a laudable object but I may, as an aside, say it would be more encouraging or more invigorating to our democracy if we could encourage those who are in their constituencies and who do not take the trouble to exercise the franchise, to do so. However, the fact that we have these people in our constituencies who do not wish to exercise their franchise is in no way an argument against enlarging the opportunities for those who do wish to vote.
I understand that the adoption of this principle would require the adoption of a permanent voters' list, because under the present system where enumerators go out at a time specified in the act after the writs of election have been issued, only those who are contacted or put on the list by the enumerators, can vote at a particular election. Hence it would be more than probable that those who would be out of the riding on construction work, or engaged in commerce, would be apt

to be missed under our present system. A voters' list of the permanent type would overcome the difficulty in our present system where so many people are left off the list and have to be put on afterwards. It seems that under the present system those who are roomers or who live in apartments are the ones who are most often left off, and it has even been found that landlords who have roomers do not encourage those living in their houses to be put on the voters list and have sometimes purposely not given their names to the enumerators, for reasons which are connected with taxation. The provision of a permanent list, as would be required by a bill such as this, would overcome these difficulties.
However, there would be some objections to a permanent list, and one of these would be the cost of maintaining such a list. It would have to be revised periodically and even then, although it might be completed close to a date, say in February, if an election were to come in January there would have to be an opportunity for making additions. I think also that difficulties would arise in areas such as Toronto where there is a constant change in the population. These changes would result in people being on the permanent list yet having moved to another place, and one would have to be careful to ensure that abuses would not arise because of the fact that people might be on two or three lists.
However, these are details which would have to be taken care of if this system were adopted, and I think that any reasonable method could be adopted if we were sincere in trying to put it into effect.
May I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND ABSENTEE VOTING PROVISIONS
speechtext: The hour for the consideration of private and public bills having expired, the house will revert to the consideration of the business which was interrupted at five o'clock.

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. C-34, to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act-Mr. Fulton -Mr. Rea in the chair.
It being six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
On clause 41-Notice of appeal.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. When the committee rose we were discussing an

amendment to clause 41. Is the committee ready for the question on the amendment?

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at five o'clock I had asked the minister a question concerning allowing sufficient time to deal with the procedure of appeal after the transcription had been made. I see that clause 41 makes ample provision for that, but I should like to draw to the minister's attention the fact that while the clause is very anxious for the accused to be diligent in making his appeal there is nothing in the clause which speaks of the diligence with which the appeal should be processed. Since, in answer to a question of the hon. member for Megantic, the minister stated that the prisoner is kept in custody if he makes a statement about his desire to go to appeal, I think it would be appropriate for provision to be made that such an appeal should be proceeded with diligently. There is nothing in the legislation which provides for that. It is quite possible that after an accused has given his notice of appeal, the appeal may just drag, things may intervene and the prisoner will be kept in custody all the time. In our language before the courts we say "kept in custody without bail". I do not think that is the intention of the minister or of the legislation. I therefore want to move the following amendment to clause 41, which is seconded by the hon. member for Megantic:
That clause 41, of Bill C-34 be further amended by adding at the end of the said clause the following words:
"and such appeal shall be proceeded with diligently within eight days from the service of such notice of appeal."

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. We have an amendment that will have to be disposed of first.
I beg your pardon. I will reserve mine until after the first amendment is disposed of.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the first amendment?
Amendment agreed to.

Without repeating what I
said Mr. Chairman, I want to suggest to the minister the following amendment to clause 41, namely that it be further amended by adding at the end of the said clause the following words:
"and such appeal shall be proceeded with diligently within eight days from the service of such notice of appeal."
The reason I make it eight days is that the notice of appeal has to be given very expeditiously, and in the meantime the prisoner is kept in custody without bail. Therefore, it would only be fair to make some provision
R.C.M.P. Act
to deal with the appeal expeditiously. However, if the minister should find that eight days would not give sufficient time-I am not familiar with the procedure in processing these things in the department-perhaps he would suggest a further delay, but the delay should be fixed within which the appeal should be heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the intent and the object of the hon. gentleman. I do not like to keep on suggesting that these things must all be left to the discretion of the officers administering the force, though I think such matters generally can be. However, I should be reluctant to accept the eight-day limitation because the appeal has to be forwarded to Ottawa, has to be processed here and then whatever proceedings are to be held must be arranged for at the place where the trial was held. I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would consent to leaving a certain discretion with the commissioner, but making it clear that the appeal must be dealt with quickly. That might be accomplished by changing the proposed amendment to read, "and such appeal should be proceeded with, with all due dispatch"? If that would be acceptable I would be very glad to accept the amendment.
I am prepared to go along in my thinking with the minister's suggestion and have confidence in the commissioner that such an appeal will be dealt with as speedily as possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
With the unanimous consent of the committee, the hon. member for Cartier would like to change his amendment to read as follows:
That clause 41, of Bill C-34 be further amended by adding at the end of the said clause the following words:
and such appeal shall be proceeded with, with all due dispatch."

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Clause 42 agreed to.
On clause 43-Board of review.

On this clause, I wonder whether the minister finds that the word "and" in the second line is necessary? It seems to me to be a bit superfluous. It says:
There shall be a board of review appointed by the minister and consisting of a deputy commissioner-
And so on. I do not see the purpose of the word "and" there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would be quite content if my hon. friend wishes to move to delete the word.

R.C.M.P. Act
Yes, I will move that the word "and" in the second line of clause 43 be deleted. The motion is seconded by the hon. member for St. Denis.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will just write it out if my hon. friends do not mind.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cartier moves:
That subclause (1) of clause 43 be amended by deleting the word "and" in line 17 on page 13 of the bill.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 43 as amended carry?
We were dealing with clause 43 (1). There is a second subclause which I would like to say a word on. Are we dealing with subclause 2, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Yes.

Subclause 2 speaks of appeals by persons convicted of a major service offence. Is there any explanation why this right to have the case dealt with is given only to those convicted of a major service offence and not to those convicted of a minor service offence?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-
If the minister will excuse me, I will complete my question. Does that mean that a person convicted of a minor service offence has no right of appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I think this was explained when we were discussing the bill on second reading at which time I pointed out that there are now created two categories of offences, major offences and minor offences. Major offences now are only those offences against the provisions of the act as set out in clause 25. These are serious offences. Minor offences are minor disciplinary offences against the standing orders, rules or regulations of the force and they carry with them a difference as to the maximum penalty that may be imposed. With respect to the major offences, it is provided that they shall all be reviewed by a board of review. With respect to minor offences, it is provided that they are automatically reviewed by the commissioner.

Under clause 43, subclause 2, I see that the board of review shall examine the record and shall make its recommendation to the commissioner. Does that mean that the offender who is appealing from the verdict and sentence will not be heard by the board of review?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no right of personal hearing. It is impossible due to distance and

a variety of other factors, but the board of review itself reviews all records, the transcript and the whole proceedings.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On clause 44-Powers of commissioner on appeal.

I may be wrong in my interpretation and I would be grateful for any enlightenment the minister can give. Under subclause 2 of the preceding clause it is clear that any appeal that is taken must be before this board of review, and at first glance I thought that clause 44 must mean that any of the powers given to the commissioner in the clause would be pursuant to a recommendation made by the board of review. I am wondering, however, whether that is the case. In the case of the quashing of a conviction, under this clause would the conviction be quashed by the commissioner only in cases where there was such a recommendation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. There may be cases in which the commissioner quashes a conviction irrespective of the recommendation of the board.

That was that I thought. The minister may have a very good explanation but as provision is made for appeal in respect of major offences one would think that this power given to the commissioner was a pretty wide power, and likewise with respect to dismissing an appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I point out to my hon. friend that he will perhaps observe that the powers of the commissioner do not extend to increasing the sentence or the severity of the sentence or the punishment imposed in any way. The powers of the commissioner relate to quashing a conviction, which is what we might call the exercise of clemency, or dismissing an appeal, which leaves the matter in status quo, or reducing the sentence or the amount ordered to be paid, which again is a reduction, or ordering a new trial, so that all the powers of the commissioner here are in the direction of reducing the severity of the sentence. He has no power to increase the sentence of the court or the recommendation of the board.
In other words, the powers given the commissioner are all seemingly directed in favour of the accused.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would be impossible. If it were a major service offence it would have to go to the board of review but the commissioner, as I have pointed out, also has the power and the responsibility of reviewing all convictions for minor offences and this power is intended to be exercised with respect to that type of offence.

May I ask the minister, who is certainly an able jurist, whether he can explain what the procedure will be where a prisoner has lodged an appeal and has discovered new evidence which he would like to bring before the court, so to speak. New evidence has turned up which he would like to bring before those sitting in appeal as it might assist him in winning an acquittal. Since no procedure is provided whereby evidence will be heard or argument can be made, but rather the procedure is limited only to a review of the record by the board, how can an accused obtain relief in the event of something in his favour turning up which was not known at the hearing?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In that case there would be a submission made by the accused or convicted member in the course of his appeal and if new evidence were disclosed the normal procedure would be to order a new trial. May I refer to what I said a moment ago in reply to the hon. member for Essex East.
About minor offences.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. I think I may have created the wrong impression. The power of the commissioner under clause 44 would extend to dismissing an appeal against a conviction for a major offence but the commissioner could not bypass the board. He could not order the appeal dismissed before the board of review had examined it.
But notwithstanding-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Notwithstanding the recommendation of the board of review it is true that he could still dismiss the appeal.

And the minister feels that is desirable power to give the commissioner? I realize that the officers here are not exactly in the same position that they would be in in civilian life. This is a police force and it may be desirable that the commissioner be given this power but, while I do not press the point, it does seem to me that where an appeal is given all of the advantages of the institution of an appeal
R.C.M.P. Act
ought to be afforded. It would appear that the accused may appeal to the board of review but notwithstanding the recommendation of the board the commissioner for some reason may dismiss the appeal. It is true that in (a) and (c) and (d), as the minister pointed out a moment ago, all the powers given to the commissioner there are directed in favour of the officer against whom the complaint is registered but in (b) that is not necessarily the case. Perhaps the minister might strengthen what he has already said by indicating why it is thought to be desirable that this particular power should be left in the hands of the commissioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To do that I think I have to go back to what I said on the last occasion, that these provisions all represent an enlargement of the rights of an accused and convicted member. Previously the only review made of his case was in the case where he was sentenced to a fine or imprisonment. In that event there was a review. Now we have provided that he has the right of appeal in every case, and in the case of a conviction for a major offence it is referred to a board of review. There is here, therefore, nothing new in retaining in the commissioner's hands the power to dismiss an appeal, but he would be extremely unlikely to dismiss an appeal in the face of a direct recommendation by a board of review.
I do point out, however, dealing with the question directly, that there may be cases of breach of discipline of such a nature that it is conceivable that, notwithstanding the recommendation of the board of review, the commissioner might feel that he still has to dismiss the appeal, or the sentence may be a reduction in rank and the commissioner might feel that in the interests of discipline of the force as a whole he must insist upon the sentence being carried out.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 45-Fine fund.

Clause 45 deals with the disposition of pecuniary penalties imposed under subsections 1 and 2 of section 36, which deals with punishment. The clause goes on to say that these penalties shall form a fund to be managed by the commissioner, with the approval of the minister, to be used for the payment of rewards for good conduct or meritorious service.
Clause 23 of this bill provides that all fines and the proceeds of all forfeitures and seizures shall be paid to the minister, and by subclause 3 the money is paid to the benefit trust fund. Am I right in assuming

R.C.M.P. Act
that the moneys, the penalties, turned over to the minister under clause 45 are going to go into that same benefit trust fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, this fund is quite separate and apart from the benefit trust fund. My hon. friend will observe, if he looks at clause 23, that it relates to fines, forfeitures and so on which are part of the sentence of an ordinary court. Those go into the benefit trust fund. Clause 45 refers to pecuniary penalties imposed under subsections 1 and 2 of section 36 which relates to fines imposed as a result of convictions against members of the service for service offences. They are two quite different types of funds and the moneys go into two separate funds. The fine fund referred to in clause 45 is much smaller than the benefit trust fund.

Mr. Chairman, it might be of benefit to read the entire clause 23, if I may, which reads as follows:
Notwithstanding any other act, all fines and the proceeds of all forfeitures and seizures and all portions of any fine and of any forfeiture or seizure that may be awarded or adjudged to any member of the force in connection with the performance of his duties-
I would think that automatically relates to clause 45 or section 36; there is no other place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, because I think my hon. friend has missed out the significant words, "that may be awarded or adjudged to any member of the force". In other words, a fine or the proceeds of a forfeiture or seizure may be awarded or adjudged to a member of the force in connection with the performance of his duties in the course of successfully pursuing and prosecuting a case. There are still some circumstances under which that might happen, and then the fine or forfeiture is paid into the benefit trust fund.
When we come to section 36 which is read in conjunction with clause 45 it is clear that those are fines or penalties imposed on a member of the force in pursuance of a conviction for a service offence.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 46-Deserters.

This bill speaks of offenders throughout as "every member" or "the member". I take it from this that the procedure set up here for punishment is restricted to members of the force. Now, we come to clause 46 in which the language is changed and the bill now speaks of "every person", for example, who has deserted from the force. I take it that the jurisdiction over the members of the force is set out in this bill, and I take it too that beyond the

authority given in this bill the commissioner and the other officials have not criminal jurisdiction over persons other than those who are members of the force.
In the next clauses, beginning with clause 46, we are speaking only of offences committed by persons who are not members of the force. Perhaps the minister could explain where the commissioner gets jurisdiction in criminal matters over people who are not members of the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The reason for the use of the word "person" in this and succeeding clauses rather than the word "member" results from the fact that these are persons who are not members of the force. My hon. friend should know that if a member deserts he is automatically struck off strength, and desertion is a major offence, defined under clause 25 of the bill, and we will still wish to deal with the deserter from the force. However, he is no longer a member of the force and therefore he has to be described as a person who has deserted.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 47 agreed to.
On clause 48-Bribes, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have an amendment to offer to clause 48. There is an error in the drafting. If the members of the committee will read carefully they will, I am sure, appreciate that in subclause 2, line 22, the word "received" should be "given". Here we are dealing with the person who is giving a bribe to a member of the force and the offence intended by this clause is the giving or offering of the bribe to a member. I would, therefore, ask one of my colleagues if they would be kind enough to move:
That subclause 2 of clause 48 be amended by striking out the word "received'' in line 22 on page 14 and substituting the word "given" therefor.
so move.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Where are the copies of this bill, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There are some coming up from downstairs.

This clause makes a little clearer the condition which I suggested to the minister might exist because here we are describing people who are not members of the force. This measure proposes to give criminal jurisdiction over people who are not members of the force. Clause 48 to me is very clear on that point. I wonder whether the minister can say whether the commissioner or the other officers would have the authority to impose penalties which are

punishable on summary conviction or would these people be prosecuted by virtue of the provisions of the Criminal Code? If so, under what section of the Criminal Code would they be prosecuted and what would be the penalty imposed? I think the minister should clear up this conflict, as I see it, of jurisdiction in criminal matters as between the courts of the land and the commissioner and officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no conflict here at all. No jurisdiction is given to the commissioner or the minister or any other person especially under this clause. Clause 48 specifically provides that persons who are guilty of the offences enumerated in subclauses (a), (b) and (c) are guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction. This refers, of course, to the ordinary summary conviction proceedings in the criminal courts of Canada. As I am sure my hon. friend is aware, if he stops to think about the matter, there is in the Criminal Code a section which provides that in the absence of the provision of any specific penalty anyone convicted of an offence against a statute on summary conviction is liable to a fine of, I think it is, $500. However, in this case, clause 51 provides a specific penalty. It provides as follows:
51. Every person who Is convicted of an offence under this part is liable to a fine of not more than five hundred dollars or to imprisonment for six months or to both.
As I recall it, that is the same provision as is found in the summary conviction part of the Criminal Code.

I think the minister is quite correct in that matter, if I may say so with all due respect to the hon. member for Cartier. This is legislation under the guise of criminal law passed by the legislative body in our country that has the power to pass legislation dealing with what is a criminal offence. But the question that I was suggesting to the hon. member for Cartier in private is this: What do we mean by "every person", for instance, in clause 46 where we find the words "every person who has deserted from the force"? The minister said that the kind of person that was envisaged there was not necessarily an officer or a member of the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. I said he would no longer be a member of the force.
After seven days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
After seven days. The hon. member for Cartier asked the question: why do you not use the terminology which you used previously, namely "a member of the
R.C.M.P. Act
force". I explained that a person who has deserted from the force is after seven days no longer a member of the force and we therefore have used the word "person".

But in clause 48 we find the following:
48(1) Every person who
(a) gives or offers or promises to give to any member of the force any bribe, pecuniary or otherwise-
That person may well be a member of the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But "person" in this case would include "member of the force", although it is not restricted to a member of the force. This is ordinary Criminal Code terminology.

The minister will appreciate the fact that as to a deserter who has been absent for two days and who offers a bribe to someone to remedy his situation, he has not yet been a deserter for seven days and therefore is still properly a member of the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But he would also be included in the word "person".
Amendment (Mr. Hamilton, Notre Dame de Grace) agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Clauses 49 to 51 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 52-Limit on prosecution.

Clause 52 reads as follows:
No proceedings in respect of an offence under this part shall be instituted more than two years after the time when the subject matter of the proceedings arose.
Was that provision in the other bill or was it already the law? Was not the time different?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. The time for instituting proceedings was unlimited.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 53-Member of force deemed a servant of the crown.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What is the situation, for instance, in the case of a member of the force driving an automobile and where an accident arises out of that fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I say, section 60 of the Exchequer Court Act determines the rights of members of the public against servants of the crown in such circumstances.
This clause merely makes it clear that members of the force are in the same position. They have no preferred position but they are in no worse position than are other servants of the crown in respect of determining liability

R.C.M.P. Act
in any action or other proceedings against Her Majesty arising out of the act of such crown servants.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What I am wondering is this. Is there any protection for them in view of their duty? I can remember the case that concerned the R.C.A.F. where an ambulance driver in the course of his duties driving the ambulance with a patient had an accident and the crown refused to have anything to do with the matter. It cost his father $50 thousand or $60 thousand before all the litigation was ended because the crown did not assume any responsibility, even though he was acting in performance of his duties at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure that was some time ago. I am not aware of all the details but I am sure my hon. friend will be aware of the fact that the rights of ordinary citizens suing the crown for the torts of its servants were considerably enlarged by a number of amendments made to the Exchequer Court Act a few years ago. There is protection again to the member of the force or crown servants in that the provisions of sections 60 and 18 of the Exchequer Court Act, I believe, say that the servant acting in the course of his duties shall not be held to be personally liable but that the crown will pay damages. We have, of course, an overriding right in the department-we have at least with respect to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-to make a specific finding that the member should contribute to or reimburse the crown in whole or in part for the cost to which the crown has been put if in the opinion of the deputy attorney general of Canada he was himself guilty of negligence. That takes a specific finding by the deputy attorney general.
Or was acting not in the course of duty.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does this clause change the common law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At common law the crown could not be sued.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have already changed the common law by statute to provide that the crown can be sued and that the crown is liable for the torts of its servants. This clause does not change that situation and carries into effect, so far as members of the force are concerned, the changes already made by statute with respect to servants of the crown.

I understand the importance of this clause, but supposing in an action against Her Majesty it was decided by the court that the act complained of, let us say a tortious act, was not committed in the course of duty. This clause as presently drawn would still not affect the position of a member of the force who "shall be deemed to have been at such time a servant of the crown".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe my hon. friend is now asking me to comment on matters about which I have not my advisers or the books before me; but my understanding is that the crown can always defend an action on the ground that its servant was not acting in the course of his employment. I think that defence is open to the crown as well as to any civilian, and it does not change that position.

I think my hon. friend is right on that, that the crown can take such a course. But notwithstanding that, the officer in question shall continue to be a servant of the crown as this clause is presently drawn?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Then I ask is that a desirable thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think so. The fact that he was not acting in the course of his employment does not change the fact that he was a servant of the crown. There are cases at law where, for example, A is the servant of B and A acts in a manner in which he is not called upon to act in the nature of his employment, and that does not change the fact that he is still the servant of B. Perhaps I should also point out that the wording here is exactly the same as the wording of an amendment to the act passed in 1957.

Mr. Chairman, can the minister explain this situation; An officer is constantly under orders, whether he is at a particular moment performing special duties or whether he is on his way home, for example, in his car or going elsewhere not in the course of his service. He is at that time also under command, under orders. Would he then be considered to be in the performance of his duties if he commits a tort during that period?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. I think the law is quite clear. As I said a moment ago, if A is the servant of B, A may be called upon to do certain things in the course of his employment. If he does things which he is not called upon to do in the course

of his employment but which lie quite outside the scope of his employment, his employer is not liable. But the fact that he acts in a manner in which he is not called upon to act by his employment does not alter the other fact that he is the servant of B. The same with an officer of the force. He is subject to discipline and liable to orders at all times. But if, as is the ordinary case, he is called upon to keep office hours and he keeps such office hours from nine to five, and then in the course of an ordinary day, after five o'clock leaves the office to drive home-he may of course be called on the radio at any time and ordered to go somewhere else-but if in the course of driving home he has an accident involving another vehicle or a civilian pedestrian, he is still an officer of the force; but clearly the act which he committed of driving into somebody else was not committed in the course of his duties as a servant of the crown.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does this clause apply only in regard to motor accidents?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh no; to all actions carried out by members of the force.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To all acts of tort, or does it apply to contracts as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would think it would apply to actions on contract as well.
To any actions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To any action, yes. The clause says:
For the purpose of determining liability in any action or other proceeding by or against Her Majesty, a person who was at any time a member of the force shall be deemed to have been at such time a servant of the crown.

I would like to explore the minister's illustration a little further. If a person leaves his duties in his office, for example, as the minister explains, and then drives home and in the course of driving home has an accident, the minister says that under those circumstances there would be no responsibility against him personally. That officer is under command-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, with respect, I do not think I said that. I think as far as I went was that I said the action committed or engaged in by the person at that time would clearly not be in the course of his duties as a servant of the crown. I did not go on to discuss the question of liability.

That is correct; I appreciate the correction. But while he is not in the performance of his duty and commits another offence, he is nevertheless under his contract and under command still answerable and is
R.C.M.P. Act
liable to be punished by his seniors. Now, there is a conflict. Either you carry full responsibility for his actions or not. You cannot just carry partial responsibility in one case and full responsibility in another.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the officer committed a service offence, such as breach of discipline or any other offence against the regulations or act while actually not on duty during office hours, he would of course be liable to be punished; but I do not see that that alters the situation we are discussing in the context of clause 53. Mr. Chairman, I would just like to say this in case I have been guilty of unintentionally misleading the committee. I was asked whether this clause changes the common law. I believe not this clause but possibly clause 43 (a), to which I have referred already which was enacted in 1957, did change it because, as I understand it, at common law a member of the R.C.M. Police is not a servant of the crown. The new section added in 1957 makes it clear that he shall be deemed to be so for the purposes set out in the section.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the minister able to say what effect, if any, it has on the civil code of the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it would have any effect on the civil code in the province of Quebec because this provision is only put in here for the purpose of making applicable thereto sections 60 and 18 of the Exchequer Court Act, which is the only act by virtue of which a civilian can sue the crown.

I do not seem to be able to reconcile the fact that he is a servant of the crown and under its command during the entire term of his duty, yet he is not responsible for acts which he commits during the hours when he is not actually on duty. He is subject to command 24 hours a day right through the entire period and he must follow orders during that entire period. When a person is subject to the orders of his employer, the employer is responsible for any tort which he commits.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend is mistaken in the law there. Surely the situation is capable of being stated on a common sense basis. Certainly a member of the force, officer, n.c.o. or constable, is subject to call 24 hours a day. But if the orders he has received make it clear that his ordinary duties extend from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon, then that does not mean to say that he is on duty from five in the afternoon until nine the next morning unless he is specifically ordered to be on duty. He may be called out on duty, but in the absence of such a call any conduct, any action which he carries on during that period after five o'clock in the

R.C.M.P. Act
afternoon and before nine o'clock in the following morning are clearly and distinctly not actions in the course of his employment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the minister not consider that some clarification might well be made of this clause? I am particularly concerned about some of the things which have happened involving members of the armed forces under similar provisions, particularly where there have been automobile accidents and where the question of whether or not the man was on duty has arisen. It has been argued-and successfully, in some cases, where there may have been improper conduct on the part of the man or officer concerned-that he was no longer protected, and yet he was still doing the duties he was supposed to be doing. As we all know, the act was designed originally to cover conditions which, in many cases, no longer exist. If an officer on patrol were to have a serious accident even though a court were to find him partly responsible, I think the fact that he was on duty and that he was doing the job because of his orders should place some responsibility on the part of the crown. Officers involved in a situation like this should not be thrown to the wolves as has sometimes been the case, and be obliged to fight their own cases without assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have endeavoured to explain already-and I am sorry if I have not made it clear-that if a member of the force is involved in an accident in he course of carrying out his duties the crown stands behind him and there is no question of calling upon a member of the force to pay damages as an individual. The damages must be recovered in an action against the crown; the other party to the accident will sue the crown and by virtue of the provision of the Exchequer Court Act may recover damages against the crown. The crown pays the damages. The only situation in which there would be any penalty imposed upon the member of the force would be not by way of telling him that he must pay the damages but by virtue only of an express finding by the deputy attorney general that the member of the force was personally negligent and that his negligence contributed to the accident to such a degree that the crown should look to him for the recovery of the damages which it has paid to the other party. Such situations are few and far between. I should say also that the terms, to the best of my recollection, of the order in council or regulation under which such findings of the deputy attorney general are made, require the finding that the negligence of the member of the force was not of a minor character. It is only 
when the negligence is of a major nature that there would be any attempt made to recover from the member the damages for which the crown has been liable, and then only a proportion of those damages.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We agree with the explanation that the minister has given, but what I am suggesting is that the explanation is not necessarily going to be the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I tell the hon. member that it is the law at the present time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It does not say that. I do not think legal counsel could find that in this particular clause. What I am suggesting is that this protection should be written into this measure and that it be much better defined so that we do not have to refer to a lot of other precedents, regulations or orders in council, whatever they happen to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The law of the land is that the master is liable for the torts of his servants. The crown is now in the same position as an ordinary civilian in this respect, and the master cannot recover from the servant in respect of damages caused by the servant in the course of his employment unless the servant is negligent, and the policy of the government is that even in such a case we do not attempt to recover from the servant unless the negligence amounts to gross negligence, and then only a part of the damages for which the crown has been held liable.

There is a basic difference in the relationship between the ordinary employer and his employee and the relationship between the government and an officer of the R.C.M.P. I think it is wrong to assume that the relationship is the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This section which we are now discussing makes the situation the same; it makes the relationship between the ordinary master and his servant and the relationship between the crown and a member of the force exactly the same in so far as liability for torts is concerned.

That is just what we are discussing. We do not think this is a fair clause. The relationship between master and servant is different because ordinarily an employee would have working hours from, say, eight to five-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So has the member of the force.

But after working hours an ordinary employee has no master to give him orders. He is not subject to be given any commands. He cannot suddenly be called out and told to go on a mission. On the other

hand a member of the force can be ordered to do something at any time of the day or night, and he must obey that command.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Precisely.

The private employee does not have to obey any such command and he is not subject to discipline if he does not obey a command given to him after hours. That is precisely the difference as I see it, and that is what we are trying to discuss. An officer of the force is subject to be ordered to go out and do things 24 hours a day and therefore the relationship between master and servant is altogether different from what it is in private industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The crown is liable for the torts of the servant if the servant is carrying out the orders of the crown but, as I have explained, in the ordinary course of events the members of the force are not on duty between-I do not know precisely what the hours are, but I use office hours as an example-five in the afternoon and nine in the morning. They are not on duty unless specifically called. If a man is called outside those hours the crown is liable for his torts, but if he is not on duty and pursuing his own private pleasures or pursuits, then his relationship with the ordinary civilian is exactly the same as that of any other member of society, and so it should be. I can see no reason on earth why the crown should be held liable or be placed in a position where it is liable for the tortious acts of a member of the force committed without any relationship to his employment whatever.
Suppose a member were on his annual leave. He is still subject, it is true, to be called back on duty and if he received a telegram that he must report back to duty at once is my hon. friend suggesting-if his argument were carried to its logical conclusion he would be suggesting-that if that member of the force while on annual leave, holidaying on a lake, drives a motor boat negligently and recklessly and injures somebody, that the crown should be held liable? Of course not. The situation is exactly the same if the member is off duty between the hours of five in the afternoon and nine in the morning.
I ask one question. Is the officer subject to orders from his employer during the 24 hours of the day?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not unless he received a specific call. If the orders and regulations lay it down that in his detachment the office hours are from nine to five and that he is off duty in other hours, then, unless he receives a specific call or order, he is off duty.
R.C.M.P. Act
But if he gets a call he is under obligation to obey it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. And if he gets a call and in the course of discharging that call he is involved in an accident the crown is liable because he is on duty.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would like to say, Mr. Chairman, in speaking of these matters that while in the legal profession it is reasonable, I presume, to use the term "master and servant" I particularly and I think most Canadian people do not appreciate that particular term as being what we have in mind. I do not think it is something that we in Canada have in mind. Some hon. members may use it. The 65 members who are members of the legal profession may agree with it but I would suggest that the Canadian people and the House of Commons should not be hearing the employer and employee relationship referred to as master and servant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend must want to rewrite every law textbook that has ever been written because the law on that subject has been called from time immemorial the law of master and servant.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We would certainly like to see it changed in this particular clause.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 54 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
We shall go back to clause 11.
On clause 11-Civilian staff.

On clause 11, Mr. Chairman, I raised a question with the minister the other day about the status of persons who are employed in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not in the category of casual employees but on a regular basis, but who are not now civil servants. The future persons so employed are to be civil servants. But the point I raised was what was to be the status of those persons now employed and how were they to be integrated into the civil service, and were they in future to have all the rights of civil servants? I suppose the minister has an answer to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am informed that this group who are not members of the force at the present time but are known as employed civilians and are not now civil servants will be given an option to elect whether they will be civilian employees or civil servants. Then, of course, if they elect to become civil servants they will have all the advantages of the Civil Service Act. With regard to their present pension rights, they will be

R.C.M.P. Act
taken care of under the related bill dealing with the superannuation of members of the force.

What about the status of their employment? Of course, the persons who are employed on a casual basis at prevailing rates are regulated by the general law, but these persons are not. These persons, I take it, are employed at a salary under some kind of statutory authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They can continue to be employed on that basis or they may elect to become civil servants.
My point is, what is the basis? Where in the act is that basis defined?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the present act it is stated that:
The governor in council may authorize the commissioner to employ in emergencies such persons as may he necessary to perform the duties of scouts, artisans, cooks, stenographers, tailors, engineers, agents, interpreters, guides or for any other purpose or for general duty for such periods as may be required and at such rates of pay as are authorized by the minister.
That is the present law but that law is being repealed, as I understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
If those people are to have a status they must have a status under some law that has not been repealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will they not be the ones who are covered in clause 11 (1), which reads:
Subject to subsection (2), such civilian officials, clerks and employees as are necessary for carrying out the functions and duties of the force shall be appointed or employed under the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
Those persons who are employed at the present time as employed civilians are employed under the provisions of the clause I just read from the present bill. I will not say they have not a status but it will be noted that they are employed for such purposes as may be required and at such rates of pay as are authorized by the minister, so they have in a sense no protected status.

I do not think the minister appreciates my point. I know that until this bill passes and he proclaims it these people can continue to be employed under the old status, but when it is proclaimed and that status disappears there will be no authority that I have been able to find anywhere that provides for the continued employment of these people in any way except the civil service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend has read clause 11 (2), because this clause provides that:

The commissioner may employ such number of temporary civilian employees at such remuneration and upon such other terms and conditions as are prescribed by the treasury board, and may at any time dismiss or discharge any such employee.
But when we have the new act in force all the present employed civilians will become either civil servants under 11 (1) or continue as civilian employees under 11 (2).
Temporary employees; in other words, they are all temporary employees at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, all those who are not civil servants and members of the force are temporary employees.

The minister said that those persons who are employed regularly the year round would be given the option of remaining under the status they have now or of becoming civil servants. Will they be expected, before becoming civil servants, to pass any special test; or, in view of their long service, will they simply be integrated into the civil service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They would, of course, have to pass the ordinary civil service requirements before they would be entitled to be integrated into the civil service under 11 (1); and if they could not pass those requirements, then they would continue to be employed as civilian employees under 11 (2).

In other words, although those persons may be performing the service satisfactorily and they may have reached relatively an advanced age where they would not have much aptitude for examinations, they will never be anything except temporary civil servants, unless they can pass the tests that a new entry to the service would have to pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, they will not be some nondescript, grey shadowy group. If my hon. friend will look at clause 7 (2) he will see that those persons contemplated under 11 (2) will fit into the situation there described, namely:
The ranks and grades of members other than officers, and the maximum numbers of persons to be appointed to each rank and grade shall be as prescribed by the treasury board.
Yes, but they will still be temporary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They will be or may be what is described as civilian members of the force.
But they cannot be brought under the superannuation act. It would appear so. Can they?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that is provided for in the other bill, yes, and we shall look for that when we go through it.
I think the minister has satisfied all my questions.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 19-Municipal bylaws.
Clause 19 is of a general character and clause 20 is more specific. I would suggest to the committee that we should deal with clause 20 and then revert to clause 19, if that is agreeable.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall we deal with clause 20 first?
Are we on clause 19?

No; it is suggested that we deal with clause 20 first.
On clause 20-Arrangements with provincial and municipal governments.

I will not read clause 20 in full but in line 8 there is a reference to "the laws in force therein", and "therein" means the municipality or the province. I should like to ask the minister if that includes by-laws.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With respect to contracts for municipal policing, it is a standard clause in every contract that the members of the force will not be responsible for carrying out the provisions of any certain municipal bylaws, and that is by virtue of the provisions of clause 19 which reads as follows:
Unless authorized by the governor in council, members shall not be charged with any duties under or in connection with any municipal by-laws.
Therefore contracts with municipal authorities have to spell out specifically what municipal by-laws members may be responsible for enforcing, if any.
Do the different agreements with provinces and municipalities include by-laws?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have here, for instance, a standard clause from one of the municipal contracts which provides that the unit shall perform such duties and render such services and no others as are ordinarily performed by police constables in aiding the administration of justice, and specifically the unit will not be called upon to engage in the issuing of licences, collection of licence fees or inspection regarding licences, in the collection of taxes or costs other than fines and costs, the impounding of cats, dogs and/or other animals, carrying out of inspections in respect of by-laws relating to health, sanitation or fire. We specifically provide that the members will not be responsible for that type of duty.
R.C.M.P. Act

But if it does happen that a municipality has the right to enact a by-law with respect to speed-ordinarily that is a provincial matter but sometimes a municipality has the power-would the mounted police acting as the municipal force be allowed to lay a charge because the speed by-law had been broken?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would be the type of by-law for which we would accept responsibility and that would be covered by the words of the contract.
I think it is nine provinces that have agreements-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Eight.
Eight provinces. Are the agreements the same or is there a difference and, if so, what is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provisions of the contract are in the main similar with the exception of Saskatchewan and Alberta where, as my hon. friend will appreciate, the history of the contracts between the force and the provinces run back appreciably farther than it does in respect to any of the other provinces.

I would be inclined to suggest, if it were not for certain circumstances that will be in the minds of all members, that there should be substituted for this clause a wholly new clause making a standard contract with the provinces part of the law laid down by parliament. The reason, of course, why I make the suggestion that this is desirable will be obvious to every hon. member. I do not intend to enter into those reasons unless I am asked to do so. There is, however, as hon. members are well aware, a case before the courts involving the interpretation of one of these contracts and I realize that it would be ridiculous to ask parliament at this time, while that action is before the courts, to lay down standard terms under which agreements could be made so that everyone would know what the law really was and would know that it had been made by parilament. But I do think this is desirable and I do not think anyone in parliament should be satisfied unless it is done at the earliest opportunity.
For that reason, sir, I intend to propose an amendment that a third subclause be added to this clause to the effect that the power given to the minister under this clause shall not extend beyond December 31, 1960. I am not moving the amendment yet. I want to explain why I have picked that particular date. In all human probability, however slow the courts may be, this action should surely be concluded by that date, but if the minister thinks that is improbable and would prefer to have a somewhat later date that

R.C.M.P. Act
would still be within the reasonable life of this parliament I would naturally be quite prepared to consider that such date be substituted. But it does seem to me that at the first opportunity when parliament can debate freely the question involved in clause 20, which we cannot do now, legislation should be brought before parliament and parliament itself should determine the conditions upon which this very unusual and extraordinary power is at the present time given not to the governor in council but to the minister with the approval of the governor in council.
This is a very great power indeed to be given to a minister, the power to provide by contract the police force of another jurisdiction which under our constitution is a sovereign jurisdiction and to make a force for which this parliament pays, for which the taxpayers of Canada pay, available to another jurisdiction and under the exclusive control, because that is what sovereignty means, of that other jurisdiction for provincial purposes. It does seem to me that this is something which grew up over a period of time mainly under the initiative of Liberal governments, I admit, and I have no apology to make for that, and about which until recently no one perhaps thought there would ever be any serious question. But a question having arisen it seems to me that in a matter of relationships that are fundamental to confederation itself parliament, not a minister even with the approval of the governor in council, should lay down the fundamental conditions-
Oh, stop wasting time.
Would the hon. member, who favours us so frequently with his intellectual efforts like to take my place and speak for a while? I am quite willing to sit down.
My intellectual efforts, really, I have to sit here and listen-
You do not have to sit here, you can leave.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

The hon. gentleman having exercised himself, perhaps I can now continue in what I believe is still a free parliament. I suggest that in order to meet this particular situation in which we find ourselves at the present time, when it would not be proper to debate the merits of these contracts or the issues involved in them-I am the first to recognize that-parliament should not give power to the minister beyond a reasonable period that may be necessary for the resolution of this question in the courts and that we should incorporate this

limitation, a limitation of a character with which the minister will be very familiar because it is precisely the kind of limitation that he urged upon the previous government with respect to other legislation.
I therefore move:
That to clause 20, subclause 3, there shall be added as follows: The power given to the minister in this section shall not extend beyond December 31, 1960.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have to make it clear that I could not accept the amendment. I should like to give my reasons, but before doing so I should like to correct another of the historical inaccuracies of the member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The hon. gentleman said that contracts with the provinces for the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I think he said were started by- I do not know whether those were his exact words, but the impression he left is that they were created, in the main, by Liberal governments.
My hon. friend is, as usual, quite inaccurate. The great majority of the contracts were started between 1932 and 1935 under the commissionership of Sir James Mac-Brien, who was appointed by the late R. B. Bennett. I have not made an historical check, but I think I am right in saying that, with respect to every province with which we now have a contract, except British Columbia, Newfoundland and Saskatchewan, the first, contracts were made under the commissionership of Sir James MacBrien between the years 1932 and 1935.
Would the minister permit a question on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Was not the first contract made with Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.
Was it not made before Sir James MacBrien was commissioner?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REVISE AND CONSOLIDATE CERTAIN PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the election of March 31, 1958 Reverend Dan Mclvor said to me, "Whatever you do in Ottawa, I want you to put on the order paper a resolution for legislation to increase pensions of civil servants and R.C.M.P. who were retired when salaries were low, so as to bring such pensions more in line with those of the present". I therefore did so. However, unfortunately, this resolution will not be reached before the end of the session for 1959.

I am sure those hon. members who knew Reverend Dan Mclvor will agree with me when I say that there is no greater humanitarian that I know of in Canada than the reverend gentleman who represented the constituency of Fort William for 23 consecutive years. He always championed the cause of the helpless, the sick and the poor. I am glad to report that he celebrated his 86th birthday a couple of months ago in good health and although retired he still shows a keen interest in the doings of the House of Commons.
It should not, therefore, surprise anyone if I am particularly happy to participate in the debate on this bill which was so close to the heart of my predecessor. It is truly my purpose to do all I can on behalf of those whom this bill is designed to benefit. I commend those responsible for its introduction at this session, even though the long wait for it has been an added burden to those concerned.
This bill will authorize the minister to appoint a Royal Canadian Mounted Police pension board. I think this is a step in the right direction.
In speaking in support of the bill I could do no better justice than to quote from what was said by my distinguished predecessor when he first introduced the measure in March of 1957. I am quoting from page 1844 of Hansard of 1957. He said:
This resolution is very simple. It deals with men and women who gave long service in the armed forces, in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and in the civil service at a time when wages were low. Conditions of service then were not what they are today. There was no 40-hour week; people had to work ten hours a day. One section of the civil service, the postmen, were on duty six days a week, and when snow was on the streets and the streets were not cleared they often worked more than ten hours a day, though they never received any overtime pay.
More than two years later conditions are far worse in so far as the value of the present dollar is concerned. No one can deny the fact that the cost of living has risen to the point where the majority of our superannuated civil servants-and I include many others-are now caught in a vicious cost-price squeeze forcing many of them to recourse to welfare agencies. It is quite evident that inflation has inflicted more hardships on retired pensioners than on business or industry. High cost of living and inflation are like Siamese twins, inseparable, and no amount of talk to the contrary can make one believe that we are not now going through a period of destructive inflation, exacting the highest price from those least able to withstand the onslaught.

In support of what I am saying now I have only to quote the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) as reported on page 1855 of Hansard of March 4, 1957. He said:
We are all conscious of rising living costs and the inflation which faces us at the present time. We know that some attempts have been made by the government to check this inflation. After having given it the original impetus by the tremendous spending of the various government departments, they are frantically trying to adjust the brakes in order to stop the runaway car to which they gave the original push. However, inflation is here, and something has got to be done for these senior retired civil servants.
If the government is not able to check inflation, then it seems to me only fair and just that the government must find some other means of helping those who are really the underprivileged class of the nation. I could read a number of letters I have received from Vancouver island during this session pointing out the plight of these people, but I shall not take up the time of the house by doing so. I merely repeat that these elderly men and women who have served this country in numerous capacities in the past are now in desperate straits. It is only by increasing their pension at the present time that some measure of relief can be brought to them, until such time as the government is able to check this inflationary trend.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if these were the conditions existing two years ago, ably reported by the present Minister of National Defence at that time, conditions now are such that the problem has become one of urgency. His reference to the inflation apparent at the time is of double import now. His statement was to the effect that the then government was not able to check inflation; but we can all agree that it made a good try and that had they been returned to power I believe conditions would be different today.
A well known professor of economics at Queen's University, appearing before a Senate committee recently, made the observation that the whole purpose of inflation is to "gyp the saver". In other words, stealing from those dependent on set incomes or pensions. Three years ago the danger of inflation made its appearance and promptly the government of the day took measures to restrain it. The opposition at that time accused the government of adopting a tight money policy and with remarkable success made the majority of the people believe that it was so and won the approaching elections.
Now, because of a heavy federal deficit which did not exist then, we face large scale unemployment plus inflation. I suggest in all seriousness that in order to safeguard the incomes of our pensioners and the stability of our dollar the government should undertake a study of the trend of inflation in Canada and put into effect ways and means to stop inflationary trends which are now beginning to affect the saving habits of our people.
