Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Transpori):
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises as follows:
1.	No.
2.	St. Lambert, Cote Ste. Catherine and Beauharnois locks filling and emptying time:
The time required to fill or empty a lock is governed by two basic factors: (1) the volume of water to be let in or out. This is directly proportional to the height of lift, and differs at the various locks; (2) the average rate of flow of the water into or out of the lock. This is controlled by the extent to which the taintor valves are opened.
Inherent to the filling characteristics of a lock is the development of a longitudinal surge, accompanied by transverse currents, which act upon a ship to different degrees, dependent upon the size and shape of the ship's hull, and dependent upon the rate of filling. Seaway locks and their hydraulic
systems have been designed to reduce these forces to within practicable limits.
Also inherent to the operating characteristics of a lock is the over-filling and overemptying which is directly proportional to the rate of filling or emptying, and which results in a reverse head acting on the upper or the lower gates, tending to open them. To avoid undue stresses in the operating mechanism, the normal procedure of opening the gate is commenced by the lock operator at about the same time as the reverse head commences to act. This procedure has been adopted at the American locks and at the Welland canal locks.
Prior to the opening of the seaway to shipping on April 25, all lock facilities, including the mitre gates, taintor valves and their operating mechanisms were subjected to mechanical, electrical and hydraulic tests to make certain that they would withstand the maximum loads for which they were designed. The test loads for the operating mechanism were appreciably greater than the actual operating loads to which they will be subjected. Tests were conducted by fully qualified engineers under the direct supervision of the structural engineer, the assistant hydraulic engineer and/or electrical-mechanical engineer. Although during the course of the tests some defects were observed, they were of a minor nature and all were remedied without difficulty.
Naturally, it was not possible to conduct complete operating tests with ships in the locks, nor was it possible to fully train the operators until after the opening of the seaway to shipping. It was decided, therefore, that until this could be completed, the rate of filling and emptying should be restricted, so that the surges in the locks and the reverse heads on gates would be of insignificant magnitudes. 1.	Have plans and specifications been prepared and finalized for the heating of the new terminal building at Dorval airport?
2.	If so, when were tenders called for the new heating outlay and to whom, and at what date was the contract awarded?
3.	What is the amount of the said contract?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
1. Design of a new central heating plant and distribution system for the new terminal building and various other buildings at the Dorval airport is being carried out by consulting engineers.
2 and 3. Tenders for boilers and ancillary equipment closed on May 1, 1959, and are now being evaluated by the consulting engineers. It is expected that tenders will be called for the distribution system within the next month, and for the remainder of the plant and building within three months.

D.B.S. REPORT  LISTING OF ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
1.	Does the government's report of the industry and merchandising division of the dominion bureau
of statistics list the Atlantic provinces separately or as a group?
2,	If listed as a group will the government give consideration to listing the provinces separately?
Answer by: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister
of Trade and Commerce):
1.	The industry and merchandising division of the dominion bureau of statistics publishes a number of reports which provide data for each of the Atlantic provinces separately. In some reports issued by the dominion bureau of statistics data must be consolidated and statistics published for the Atlantic provinces as a group.
2.	Where resources are available and where the data published by the dominion bureau of statistics does not disclose the operations of an individual plant or company, every effort is made to show statistics for each of the Atlantic provinces separately. In some instances, the limitations of source data do not permit the refinement and publication of figures for the Atlantic provinces separately. For instance, in the case of retail trade, until recently, the estimates of sales for intercensal periods were provided for the Atlantic provinces as a whole. However, steps have been taken to enlarge the monthly and annual surveys by the addition of 4,000 stores, which will permit the preparation of estimates for all Atlantic provinces separately.

Wednesday, June 24, 1959
